{"id": "1:1/q10", "question": "From what is ٱللَّهِ derived?", "turns_on": "Whether Allāh is an underived proper name or a contracted or otherwise derived form.", "positions": [{"id": "1:1/q10/p1", "position": "Allāh derives from al-ilāh or ilāh through loss of hamza and assimilation.", "reasons": "TAB (author): Allah’s form comes from al-ilāh: the initial hamza is dropped, then the two lām sounds meet and assimilate into one doubled lām. TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī proposes that Allāh derives from al-ilāh: the initial hamza is dropped and the adjacent lām sounds assimilate into one doubled lām. THALABI (أهل الكوفة): The Kufans derive Allah from ilāh: the definite article magnified the name, then the hamza dropped through frequent use and the two lām letters assimilated. MAWARDI-FULL (author): A second view derives Allah from ilāh: the hamza is dropped and the pronunciation intensified. JISHUMI (سيبويه): One derivation takes Allah from ilāh, dropping the hamza and making the alif-lām an obligatory substitute so the name becomes a proper name. KASHSHAF (author): Allah derives from al-ilah, with hamza removed; al-nas likewise derives from al-unas, with the hamza replaced by the article. IBNATIYYA (author): Three accounts explain the change from ilah to Allah: irregular loss of hamza before alif-lam, alif-lam added to ilah with hamza-vowel transfer and lam assimilation, or an original lah; Ibn Atiyya favors the first. IBNATIYYA (الخليل): Al-Khalil says the original was ilah or walah, with hamza substituted for waw as in ishaḥ/wishaḥ and isadah/wisadah. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Several analyses explain the development from ilah to Allah through deletion or movement of the hamza and attachment of the article; the author judges the first explanation strongest. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الخليل): Al-Khalil reports that ilah/walah began with wāw, with hamza substituted as in ishaḥ/wishaḥ and isādah/wisādah. RAZI-FULL (الكوفيون): The Kufans derive Allah from ilāh with the article for glorification, then explain loss of hamza and assimilation of the two lām letters. QURTUBI (الخليل وسيبويه): Al-Khalīl and Sibawayh derive Allah from ilāh, with the article replacing hamza, as nās derives from unās. BAYDAWI (author): Allāh is said to derive from ilāh, with hamza deleted and replaced by the article; ilāh originally meant any deity but came to designate the true deity. NASAFI (author): Allah derives from al-ilah, like al-nas from al-unas: the hamza drops and the definite article substitutes for it. Ilah once named any true or false object of worship, then chiefly the true one; Allah without hamza is exclusive to the true God. NASAFI-FULL (author): Allah is uniquely the name of the true God, not an attribute; the source derives it from al-ilah with hamza loss, while Khalil, al-Zajjaj, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl deny derivation and other accounts link it to bewilderment or worship. SAMIN-DURR (author): On the al-ilah derivation, hamza is dropped through frequent use, like anās becoming nās; an alternative account transfers its vowel before deletion. IBNKATHIR (الخليل وسيبويه): Al-Khalil and Sibawayh derive the word from ilah, with the article replacing an initial hamza, by analogy with al-nas from unas; another proposal takes it from lah for exalted. IBNKATHIR (الكسائي والفراء): Al-Kisaʾi and al-Farraʾ derive it from al-ilah, with the hamza dropped and the two lams assimilated, like lakinna from lakin ana. | mentions 18:38 IBNKATHIR (author): The proposed form begins as al-ilah; deleting the hamza brings two lams together, which assimilate and are pronounced as one emphatic doubled lam. ALUSI (author): Authorities derive Allāh either from al-ilāh or ilāh with hamza loss and compensatory alif-lām; Ibn Mālik instead argues for a distinct root and original proper name. ALUSI (ابن مالك): Ibn Mālik denies that Allāh derives from al-ilāh, arguing their forms and meanings differ and that deletion or hamza transfer lacks a sound morphological parallel. ALUSI-FULL (الصحاح والكشاف): The lexicons differ between deriving Allah from al-ilāh and ilāh; al-Alusi says the hamza was most likely dropped without a regular cause and replaced by the article. ELMALILI (Kûfiyyûn): The Kufans derive Allah from al-ilāh, with the article becoming integral and its hamza compensating for the elided hamza of ilāh; ilāh is linked to worship, awe, tranquility, or release from fear. {"id": "1:1/q11", "question": "Is ٱللَّهِ a proper, underived name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "1:1/q11/p1", "position": "Allāh is a proper name for God's unique essence, not a derived description.", "reasons": "THALABI (الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة): Al-Khalil and others say Allah is a proper name, not derived; the verse “Do you know any namesake for Him?” supports its unique reference. | mentions 19:65 MAWARDI (unattributed): One view treats Allah as an un-derived proper name for the divine essence, needed as the name to which attribute names attach. MAWARDI-FULL (author): One view treats Allah as a proper name for the divine essence, not derived from an attribute, since attribute names depend on an essence name. WAHIDI-QT (author): Allah is a name unique to the Creator, functioning like a proper name and having no known derivation. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Allah is God's unique proper name, functioning like a proper name among His names, with no known derivation. BAGHAWI (الخليل): Al-Khalil and others treat Allah as a proper name specific to God, not derived, like human names Zayd and ʿAmr. BAGHAWI-FULL (الخليل وجماعة): Al-Khalil and a group treat Allah as a proper name unique to God, with no derivation, like human proper names. KASHSHAF (author): Allah is a proper name, not an attribute; it is predicated of things but does not describe them, and divine attributes require a named subject. IBNATIYYA (فرقة من أهل العلم): One group of scholars treats Allah as an un-derived proper name, with alif-lam integral to the name rather than a marker of definiteness. TABRISI (الخليل): Al-Khalil treats Allah as an un-derived proper name, arguing that not every word must have a derivation or derivation would regress forever. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (العلماء): Scholars disagree whether the divine name Allāh is derived or an underived proper name. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الخليل): One view attributed to al-Khalīl says Allāh is not derived and its alif-lām cannot be dropped as it can from al-Raḥmān. RAZI-FULL (author): The closest view is that 'Allah' is the greatest name because it functions as a proper name for God and denotes His unique essence. RAZI-FULL (author): Razi says Allah is a proper name, then asks whether that name itself signifies the divine attributes. RAZI-FULL (author): Razi's chosen view is that Allah is a proper name for God, not a derivative; he attributes it to al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, and most legal theorists and jurists. RAZI-FULL (author): If Allah were derived, it would denote a general concept open to many bearers, making “There is no god but Allah” fail to establish exclusive monotheism; its established force proves it is a proper name. RAZI-FULL (author): A proper name normally precedes descriptive predicates; likewise speakers say “Allah, the Knowing, the Powerful,” not the reverse. RAZI-FULL (author): The apparent counterexample in Ibrahim 14:1 has two readings: nominative makes Allah a new subject, while genitive identifies which praised one is meant rather than making a proper name into an adjective. | mentions 14:1 RAZI-FULL (القائلون بأنه ليس اسم علم): Opponents argue that “He is Allah in the heavens” and “He is Allah” use Allah predicatively, unlike a proper name such as Zayd. | mentions 6:3, 59:22 RAZI-FULL (author): Most accept the word as Arabic; those who deny that Allah is a proper name divide between Kufan and Basran derivations. RAZI-FULL (author): The report supports taking “Allah” as a proper name for God's unique essence, since a derived general noun could not identify that individual essence; “All-Merciful” and “Merciful” are universal terms. QURTUBI (الشافعي وأبو المعالي والخطابي والغزالي): Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Juwaynī, al-Khaṭṭābī, and al-Ghazālī treat Allah as a non-derived proper name with inseparable alif-lām.
